query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying a thin, uniform hafnium coating on the surface of boride‐based components will improve their resistance to molten‐aluminum corrosion by promoting the in situ formation of an adherent HfO2 barrier during service.
generation.material_initial_state: Standard boride-based components (e.g., high‐entropy borides or HfB2/ZrB2 ceramics) with their typical microstructure and surface finish as produced by conventional processing.
generation.intervention: Introduce a surface modification step—depositing a thin hafnium layer (via sputtering, chemical vapor deposition, or hot‐press sintering of Hf powder) onto the component prior to use in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment.
generation.conditions: Components are used in hot-dip aluminum-plating environments, where they are in contact with molten aluminum (approximately 660 °C) under conditions of moderate thermal cycling and mechanical stress typical for plating operations.
generation.structural_mediator: The hafnium coating, upon initial exposure to the oxygen potential present at elevated temperatures and during transient exposure to air/moisture in the plating bath environment, rapidly oxidizes to form a dense, adherent HfO2 layer on the surface.
generation.mechanism: HfO2 is well known for its high melting point, low oxygen permeability, and chemical inertness. The pre-deposited hafnium rapidly forms HfO2 under operational conditions, thereby acting as a protective barrier that prevents molten aluminum from directly contacting and reacting with the underlying boride matrix. This barrier limits the dissolution and corrosive attack of the component, leading to improved corrosion resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated boride components, those with the hafnium pre-coating should exhibit significantly reduced corrosion indicators—such as lower mass change (or weight loss due to spallation), less surface degradation, and a thinner or more stable corrosion product layer—after prolonged exposure to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components manufactured by conventional methods without any additional surface coating typically show measurable corrosion damage (spallation, oxide formation, and potential material loss) when in contact with molten aluminum during hot-dip plating.
generation.boundary: This intervention is anticipated to be effective under typical hot-dip aluminum plating temperatures (around 660 °C) and in conditions where mechanical abrasion and extreme thermal cycling are limited to those common in plating operations. Its efficacy in environments with significantly higher operational stress or lower oxygen partial pressures remains to be verified.
generation.uncertainty: This hypothesis builds on observations from a study (PMC10488483) showing that a hafnium-coated high-entropy alloy achieved improved high-temperature oxidation resistance via the formation of a protective HfO2 layer, and on reports (PMC10608203) suggesting that Hf-rich borides enhance stability at high temperatures. Extending these findings to molten-aluminum corrosion in plating operations is plausible but unproven; the exact kinetics of oxide formation and long-term barrier integrity in a molten metal environment are not yet well established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of identical boride-based test samples. Apply a thin hafnium coating to one group while leaving the other group uncoated. Expose both sets to controlled molten aluminum baths maintained at approximately 660 °C for varying durations (e.g., 5, 10, and 20 hours) under identical environmental and thermal cycling conditions. Post-exposure, systematically characterize the samples.
measurements: Mass change measurements to assess weight gain/loss due to oxidation or spallation
Surface morphology and oxide scale characterization using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS)
Corrosion depth profiling (e.g., via profilometry or cross-sectional analysis)
Adhesion and integrity testing of the formed oxide layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the hafnium-coated specimens do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., reduced mass change, less spallation, or thinner/better-adherent oxide layers) compared to the uncoated specimens under the same molten aluminum exposure conditions.

cited_evidence.text: High-temperature oxidation-resistant VZrHfNbTa refractory HEA-based Hf-coated composites are prepared by the combined process. It has a coating thickness of 120 μm. Vanadium, niobium, tantalum and hafnium elements in the base alloy have obvious boundaries with the hafnium coating, and the zirconium element undergoes diffusion and migration in the coating with a diffusive distance of about 60 μm. High-temperature oxidation tests show that the weight gain per unit area of the coated sample is much less than that of the uncoated sample. Dents and pulverization on the surface of the alloy after oxidation of the uncoated specimen, oxidation, and sintering on the surface of the coated specimen result in the formation of a dense HfO2 protective layer. The coating can effectively improve the oxidation resistance of the material in extreme environments and prevent the surface from chalking, thus extending the material’s service life and broadening the application. Increasing the temperature range of operation and energy load of machines and mechanisms requires the creation of new generation materials. Such materials should have an optimal combination of mechanical, thermophysical, and chemical properties: high hardness, thermal conductivity, crack resistance, oxidation and corrosion resistance in a wide temperature range, low friction coefficient, and phase stability at elevated temperatures [,]. Most studies in this area are devoted to ZrB2, HfB2 materials, and composites based on them [,,,,,,]. Hafnium diboride has the highest melting point (3523 K) among borides, high thermal conductivity, hardness and bending strength in a wide temperature range. This applies both to single-phase hafnium diboride and to composite materials based on it. However, the mechanical properties of HfB2 significantly depend on structure and porosity [,,,].
